The above matter comes on for entry of a final order of disposition by the Oklahoma Tax
Commission. Having reviewed the files and records herein, including the Findings of Fact and
Conclusions of Law (“Findings”) entered by the Administrative Law Judge on February 27,
2017, the Commission makes the following Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law and enters
the following Order.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
On the 27th day of February 2017, the above-styled and numbered cause came on for
consideration under assignment regularly made by the Oklahoma Tax Commission to ALJ,
Administrative Law Judge. COMPANY (“Protestant”) appeared through attorneys,
ATTORNEY 1, and ATTORNEY 2, FIRM.1 The Compliance Division (“Division”) of the
Oklahoma Tax Commission appeared through OTC ATTORNEY 1, Assistant General Counsel,
and OTC ATTORNEY 2, Assistant General Counsel, Office of General Counsel, Oklahoma Tax
Commission.
This matter concerns the Division’s denial of Protestant’s claim for refund for the 2008
and 2009 tax periods based on a Net Operating Loss (“NOL”) generated during Protestant’s 2010
Tax Year (10/01/2010 – 09/30/2011). Initially, Protestant carried forward the 2010 NOL to its

Upon review of the Findings, Conclusions and Recommendations and the exhibits

Findings at 6, ¶ 2.
3. On or about February 14, 2011, Protestant filed its Oklahoma Corporation Income

ISSUES AND CONTENTIONS
The issue before the Commission for decision is whether Protestant is barred by statute
from receiving refunds of corporate income taxes for the 2008 and 2009 tax years based upon
Protestant’s failure to file claims for refund within the time prescribed by 68 O.S. Supp. 2010, §
2373. Also presented for discussion is whether the Commission may be equitably estopped from
enforcing the provisions of 68 O.S. Supp. 2010, § 2373.
The Division contends the protests to the denial of Protestant’s claims for refunds on the
2008 and 2009 amended returns should be denied because the claims were not filed timely and
are barred by statute. In support thereof, the Division argues Protestant did not file the required
election with its 2010 return to forego the two year NOL carryback period; thus, Protestant was
required to carry back the 2010 NOL to its 2008 and 2009 tax years prior to carrying forward any
remaining NOL. Further, the Division contends that in order to receive a refund for 2008 or
2009 based on a NOL carryback from 2010, Protestant needed to file amended returns for those
years by December 15, 2014—three years after the due date of the 2010 return which generated
the NOL. Protestant did not file amended income tax returns to claim refunds for 2008 and 2009
until September 2015, well beyond the three year period prescribed by 68 O.S. § 2373 for
making such claims.
Protestant contends the Division’s failure to notify it of the status of the 2011 and 2012
proposed adjustments to its returns, after it protested the proposed adjustments, precluded
Protestant from timely filing its 2008 and 2009 amended income tax returns. As such, Protestant
argues the Division should be estopped from denying its claims for refund for tax years 2008 and
2009.9
9 The Commission presumes Protestant’s estoppel argument relates to the 2008 and 2009 Amended Tax Returns, as
“[t]he Division’s adjustments to the 2011 and 2012 Tax Years are not being protested.” Findings at 8, n.21;
8 of 27 OTC ORDER NO. 2017-05-04-08

NON-PRECEDENTIAL DECISION OKLAHOMA TAX COMMISSION
The Division responds that general principles of equity may not override statutory
requirements for timely filing of tax refund claims. Brief of Division at 7, citing Republic
Petroleum Corp. v. United States, 613 F. 2d 518, 527 (5th Cir. 1980).
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
A. Jurisdiction and Burden of Proof:
1. Jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter of this proceeding is vested with
the Oklahoma Tax Commission. 68 O.S. § 207; 68 O.S. § 221(D).
2. The taxpayer has the burden of proof to show the action or proposed action of the
Oklahoma Tax Commission is incorrect, and in what respect. OAC 710:1-5-47. In re Adway
Properties, Inc., 2006 OK CIV APP 14, ¶ 9, 130 P.3d 302, 304; Geoffrey, Inc. v. Oklahoma Tax
Commission, 2006 OK CIV APP 27, ¶ 25, 132 P.3d 632, 640, citing TPQ Inv. Corp. v. State ex
rel. Oklahoma Tax Commission, 1998 OK 13, 954 P.2d 139. If the taxpayer fails to prove a
prima facie case, the protest may be denied solely on the grounds of failure to prove sufficient
facts that would entitle the taxpayer to the requested relief. OAC 710:1-5-47. Continental Oil
Company v. Oklahoma State Board of Equalization, 1976 OK 23, 570 P.2d 315, 317.
3. The burden of proof standard is “preponderance of evidence.” 2 Am.Jur.2d
Administrative Law § 357. “Preponderance of evidence” means “[e]vidence which is of greater
weight or more convincing than the evidence offered in opposition to it; that is, evidence which
as a whole shows the fact sought to be proved is more probable than not * * * evidence which is
more credible and convincing to the mind * * * that which best accords with reason and
Division’s Exhibits I and J, letters dated October 26, 2015 and November 5, 2015 from CPA, CPA, PC to
AUDITOR, Compliance Division, Oklahoma Tax Commission, at 2 (“After a review of [Rule 710:50-1-51(4)],
OTC order 2012-02-07-12 and the Form 512 instructions, the Company determined that the adjustments to the 2011
and 2012 returns were correct and paid the outstanding taxes for those years.”); see also Protestant’s Exhibits H and
J (Same). The confusion arises when referring to the Brief of Protestant which states as Issue No. 3, “Whether the
OTC should be equitably estopped to deny Accurate Drilling a tax refund on its 2011 and 2012 returns?”; and as a
Conclusion, “For the foregoing reasons, the OTC should be estopped to deny Taxpayer a refund on its 2011 and
2012 tax refund.” See Brief of Protestant, at 3, 7.

probability.” BLACK’S LAW DICTIONARY 1064 (5th ed. 1979). Each element of the claim
must be supported by reliable, probative, and substantial evidence of sufficient quality and
quantity as to show the existence of the facts supporting the claim are more probable than their
nonexistence. 2 Am.Jur.2d Administrative Law § 357.
B. Administrative Rules and Regulations:
1. Rules promulgated under the Administrative Procedures Act10 are presumed to be
valid until declared otherwise by a court of competent jurisdiction. 75 O.S. § 306(C). They are
valid and binding on the persons they affect, have the force of law and are prima facie evidence
of the proper interpretation of the matter to which they refer. 75 O.S. § 308.2(C).
2. The rules and regulations of an administrative agency which implement a statute
are valid unless they are beyond the scope of the statute, conflict with the statute or are
unreasonable. See, Boydston v. State, 1954 OK 327, 277 P.2d 138, 142. Agency rules need not
be specifically authorized by statute, but must generally reflect the intent of the Legislature as
expressed in the statute. Jarboe Sales Company v. Oklahoma Alcoholic Beverage Laws
Enforcement Commission, 2003 OK CIV APP 23, ¶ 10, 65 P.3d 289, 292. As a general rule, it is
presumed that administrative rules and regulations are fair and reasonable, and the complaining
party must prove the contrary by competent and convincing evidence. State ex rel. Hart v.
Parham, 1966 OK 9, 412 P.2d 142, 152.
3. Great weight is accorded an agency’s construction of a statute when the
administrative interpretation is made contemporaneously with the enactment of the statute and
the construction is longstanding and continuous by the agency charged with its execution.
Schulte Oil Co., Inc. v. Oklahoma Tax Commission, 1994 OK 103, 882 P.2d 65, 68. Where the
Legislature is made repeatedly aware of the operation of the statute according to the construction

placed upon it by an agency and the Legislature has not expressed its disapproval with the
agency’s construction, the Legislature’s silence may be regarded as acquiescence in the
agency’s construction, R. R. Tway, Inc. v. Oklahoma Tax Commission, 1995 OK 129, 910 P.2d
972; and the agency’s construction is given controlling weight and will not be disregarded except
in cases of serious doubt, Cox v. Dawson, 1996 OK 11, 911 P.2d 272, 279.
C. Income Tax:
1. “Taxation is an exclusively legislative function that can be exercised only under
statutory authority and in the manner specified by statute.” State ex rel. Oklahoma Tax Comm'n
v. Texaco Expl. & Prod., Inc., 2005 OK 52, ¶ 7, 131 P.3d 705, 707, citing Gay v. Thomas, 1896
OK 67, 46 P. 578 (Sup.Ct.Okla.Terr.). Accordingly, this matter is governed by the Oklahoma
Income Tax Act (68 O.S. 2011, § 2351 et seq., as amended).
2. Every corporation is required to make a return for each taxable year stating the
taxable income and the adjustments provided in 68 O.S. § 2351 et seq. to arrive at Oklahoma
taxable income. 68 O.S. § 2368(E). Fiscal year corporation returns must be made on or before
the fifteenth day of the third month following the close of the fiscal year. 68 O.S. § 2368(G)(5).
3. Every return is required to be filed with the Commission in such form as the
Commission may, from time to time, prescribe. Upon application, the Commission will furnish
the required forms; however, failure to secure or receive the form of a return prescribed shall not
relieve any taxpayer from the obligation of making and filing any required return. 68 O.S. §
2368(I).
4. A taxpayer may deduct a net operating loss from its taxable income in accordance
with section 2358(A)(3), which provides:
The amount of any federal net operating loss deduction shall be adjusted as
follows:

b. . . . For tax years beginning after December 31, 2008, the years to which such
losses may be carried back shall be determined solely by reference to Section 172
of the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C., Section 172, with the exception that the
terms "net operating loss" and "taxable income" shall be replaced with
"Oklahoma net operating loss" and "Oklahoma taxable income".
68 .S. Supp. 2010, § 2358(A)(3).
5. For Protestant’s 2010 Tax Year, net operating losses were required to be carried
back two taxable years preceding the taxable year of the loss and then carried forward to each of
the twenty taxable years following the taxable year of the loss. 26 U.S.C.A. § 172(b)(1)(A).
Under Section 172(b)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code (“IRC”), a taxpayer may elect to
relinquish the entire carryback period with respect to a net operating loss for any taxable year, if
he does so in the manner prescribed by the due date for filing the taxpayer’s return for the
taxable year of the net operating loss for which the election is to be in effect. 26 U.S.C. §
172(b)(3). Once made for any taxable year, the election is irrevocable for that taxable year. Id.
6. Oklahoma permits an election to forego the net operating loss carryback period,
provided a written statement of the election is made a part of the timely filed Oklahoma loss year
return. OAC 710:50-17-51(4). Specifically, OAC 710:50-17-51(4) provides as follows:
(4) Oklahoma net operating loss carryback/carryover. An election may be
made to forego the Net Operating Loss (NOL) carryback period. A written
statement of the election must be part of the timely filed Oklahoma loss year
return.
See also 512-S Instructions for the 2010 Tax Year, available on the Tax Commission website
at https://www.ok.gov/tax/ (July 11, 2013):
An election may be made to forgo the carryback period. A written statement of
the election must be part of the original timely filed Oklahoma loss-year return. If
the corporation timely filed its return for the loss-year without making the
election, it may make the election on an amended return filed within six (6)
months of the due date of the loss year return (excluding extensions). The

taxpayer attaches the election to the amended return. Once made, the election is
irrevocable.
See also, OTC Order No. 95-03-23-017 (Precedential). 11
D. OKLA. STAT. tit. 68, § 2373:
1. The terms of 68 O.S. § 2373 provide, in relevant part, that “ . . . the amount of the
refund shall not exceed the portion of the tax paid during the three (3) years immediately
preceding the filing of the claim, or, if no claim was filed, then during the three (3) years
immediately preceding the allowance of the refund.” 68 O.S. Supp. 2010, § 2373.
2. Regarding 68 O.S. § 2373, the Oklahoma Supreme Court has held as follows:
§ 2373 acts in a manner analogous to a statute of repose in that it acts as a
substantive limitation on the right to recover any amount as a refund when the
claim for refund is filed more than three years after the date on which Oklahoma
income tax is paid. In other words, as applicable here, § 2373 is a legislatively
crafted outer limit time boundary beyond which taxpayers’ right to recover a
refund no longer exists.
Neer v. State ex. rel. Okla. Tax Comm’n, 1999 OK 41, ¶ 2, 982 P.2d 1071, 1073, as corrected
(June 4, 1999).
3. “Judicial construction of a statute and longstanding acquiescence therein serves
to give such judicial construction the effect of legislation. The interpretation of a statute by the

highest courts of a state by which the statute was enacted is generally regarded as an integral part
of the statute.” Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. Travis, 1984 OK 33, 682 P.2d 225, 227.
4. “In Neer v. State ex rel. Oklahoma Tax Comm'n, 1999 OK 41, 982 P.2d 1071,
1080, the Oklahoma Supreme Court held the statutory period of three years begins to run from
the date the refund claim should have been filed even if all of the elements necessary to support a
viable refund claim are not present.” Matlock v. State ex rel. Okl. Tax Comm'n, 2001 OK CIV
APP 104, ¶ 3, 29 P.3d 614, 615, certiorari denied.
5. The Tax Commission and the taxpayer may sign a consent to extend the period
during which the taxpayer may file a claim for refund or during which an allowance for a refund
may be made which shall automatically extend the final date fixed by such consent plus thirty
(30) days. 68 O.S. § 2373; see also, Neer v. State ex rel. Oklahoma Tax Com'n, 1999 OK 41, ¶¶
14, 28, 982 P.2d 1071, 1077, 1081.
6. “Where a substantial part of the statutorily-prescribed time period on refund
claims remains when a taxpayer learns of events causing, or likely to cause, a decrease in his/her
tax liability, a protective refund claim should be filed during the prescribed period in order to
preserve the viability of a refund claim.” Neer v. State ex rel. Oklahoma Tax Comm'n, 1999 OK
41, ¶ 29, 982 P.2d 1071, 1082. “If a protective claim is not filed within the specified period in
such a situation, a refund claim will be barred, notwithstanding the fact that the exact amount of
a refund cannot be determined until after the time period has expired.” Id.

by 68 O.S. Supp. 2010, § 2373. The Commission orders the protest of Protestant be denied.
